{{nihongo|'''Takamu Shrine'''|高牟神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Owari Province]].

'''Takamu Shrine'' is located at {{ill|Aichi Prefecture|Q80434|qid=Q80434}}{{ill|Nagoya|Q11751|qid=Q11751}}{{ill|Chikusa-ku, Nagoya|Q1207951|qid=Q1207951}}{{ill|Imaike|Q11377165|qid=Q11377165|lt=Imaike}} {{ill|Shinto shrine|Q845945|qid=Q845945}} located in 1-chome. It is compared to {{ill|Owari Province|Q514506|qid=Q514506}}{{ill|Aichi District|Q552687|qid=Q552687|lt=Aichi District}} ``Takamu Shrine'' in ``{{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932}}''.

== History ==
According to the <ref> precincts information board, it is an old shrine that was founded in the era of {{ill|Emperor Seimu|Q316672|qid=Q316672}}, and that {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|Q317997|qid=Q317997}} was enshrined in the era of {{ill|Emperor Seiwa|Q349243|qid=Q349243}}. </ref>. Until {{ill|Early modern period|Q5308718|qid=Q5308718}}, it was called '''Hachimangu''''. It was also called ``Funade Hachiman'' because there was a {{ill|Idols in Shinto|Q11588751|qid=Q11588751}} riding on a {{ill|Watercraft|Q1229765|qid=Q1229765}}.After {{ill|1441|Q6402|qid=Q6402}} ({{ill|Kakitsu|Q1193238|qid=Q1193238}} first year), there are records of the construction and restoration of multiple shrines. The Shrines and Temples Edition includes the {{ill|Kanshō|Q1143928|qid=Q1143928}} 2nd year ({{ill|1461|Q6532|qid=Q6532}}) and {{ill|Tenbun|Q1192853|qid=Q1192853|lt=astronomical}} 1st year ({{ill|1532|Q6436|qid=Q6436}}), {{ill|Eiroku|Q1143341|qid=Q1143341}}8th year ({{ill|1565|Q6634|qid=Q6634}}) and {{ill|Keichō|Q1328185|qid=Q1328185}}8th year ({{ill|1603|Q6735|qid=Q6735}}) are listed (p.322-325). }}, both {{ill|Munafuda|Q8008834|qid=Q8008834}} say ``Koimura Hachiman Shrine'' and ``Hachiman Shrine.'' Before {{ill|Keichō|Q1328185|qid=Q1328185}}, it was located in Genkai Village, Hakusan, west of the current location (currently {{ill|Naka-ku, Nagoya|Q1207921|qid=Q1207921|lt=Naka Ward}}{{ill|Shinei|Q11502585|qid=Q11502585}}, Hakusansha), but there is a legend that it was moved to its current location when {{ill|Nagoya Castle|Q648629|qid=Q648629}} was being built over Kiyosu|Q11561274}}. "{{ill|Kanbunmuramuraoboegaki|Q137766629|qid=Q137766629}}", which was established in the early Edo period, states, The Kojima family, who were {{ill|Negi|Q11594490|qid=Q11594490}} of Furui village, served as {{ill|Kannushi (disambiguation)|Q15888735|qid=Q15888735}} in {{ill|Early modern period|Q5308718|qid=Q5308718}}. {{ill|Owari Domain|Q1062072|qid=Q1062072}} lord {{ill|Tokugawa Mitsutomo|Q843245|qid=Q843245}} was {{ill|Tenna|Q1145289|qid=Q1145289|lt=Tenwa}}There is a record that the shrine building was repaired in 1683|Q7651}} {{Sfn|History of Chikusa Ward|1981|p=34}}{{Sfn|History of Chikusa Ward|1987|p=429}}. Until {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|Q1970535|qid=Q1970535}}, Gyokuryuzan Koshoin (still located to the east of our company) was {{ill|Jingū-ji|fr|Jingū-ji|it|Jingū-ji|ja|神宮寺|pl|Jingū-ji|ru|Дзингудзи|zh|神宮寺|qid=Q1074971}}. In {{ill|1873|Q7757|qid=Q7757}} (Meiji 5), it was ranked as {{ill|Gō-sha|Q134917316|qid=Q134917316}} in the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|Q712534|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}}. The shrine buildings were burnt down in the {{ill|Airstrike|Q2380335|qid=Q2380335}} of {{ill|Pacific War|Q184425|qid=Q184425}}, but were rebuilt after the war.It was identified by {{ill|Amano Sadakage|Q6535030|qid=Q6535030}} as ``Takamu Shrine'' in Aichi District, Owari Province, which appears in the ``Engishiki Shinmyocho,'' and it became an established theory after the mid-Edo period. In {{ill|1868|Q7717|qid=Q7717}} ({{ill|Meiji era|ar|فترة مييجي|ast|Dómina Meiji|az|Meydzi dövrü|azb|مئی‌جی دؤورو|be|Перыяд Мэйдзі|bn|মেইজি যুগ|bo|མེའི་ཇིའི་དུས་དུས་མཚམས།|ca|Era Meiji|cs|Období Meidži|da|Meiji-perioden|de|Meiji-Zeit|el|Μεϊτζί (περίοδος)|es|Era Meiji|et|Meiji periood|eu|Meiji Aroa|fa|دوره میجی|fi|Meiji-kausi|fr|Ère Meiji|gl|Período Meiji|he|תקופת מייג'י|hr|Meiji (razdoblje)|ht|Epòk Meiji|hu|Meidzsi-kor|id|Zaman Meiji|io|Ero Meiji|is|Meiji-tímabilið|it|Periodo Meiji|ja|明治|ka|მეიძის ეპოქა|kbp|Mejii wɛɛ yaa alɩwaatʊ|kk|Мэйдзи дәуірі|ko|메이지 시대|la|Aetas Meiji|lt|Meidži laikotarpis|lv|Meidzi periods|mk|Меиџи (период)|mn|Мэйжийн эрин|ms|Zaman Meiji|nl|Meijiperiode|nn|Meiji|no|Meiji-perioden|pl|Meiji (okres)|pt|Era Meiji|ro|Perioada Meiji|ru|Мэйдзи|simple|Meiji period|sk|Obdobie Meidži|sq|Periudha Meixhi|sr|Меиџи период|sv|Meijiperioden|ta|மெய்சி காலம்|th|ยุคเมจิ|tl|Panahong Meiji|tr|Meiji Dönemi|uk|Період Мейдзі|ur|میجی دور|vi|Thời kỳ Minh Trị|war|Panahon Meiji|wuu|明治|zh|明治|zh_classical|明治|zh_min_nan|Bêng-tī|zh_yue|明治|qid=Q3125096}} first year), it was officially renamed "Takamu Shrine". However, the basis for comparing our company to Takamu Shrine is not clear, and {{ill|Tsuda Masanari|Q22123474|qid=Q22123474}}, a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=local historian}} from the late Edo period, questions the idea of ​​comparing our company to ``Takamu Shrine.'' Takamu Shrines other than ours include Takamine Daimyojin (currently enshrined in {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Yagoto Shrine}}) and Takamu Shrine in {{ill|Takabari|Q50324950|qid=Q50324950}}, but both of these shrines were built before {{ill|Middle Ages|Q12554|qid=Q12554}} in {{ill|Yamada district, Owari|Q11470699|qid=Q11470699|lt=Yamada District}} Because it is within the area, it is not considered a likely candidate for Takamu Shrine in Aichi District. Masao Tsuda also lists {{ill|Gokiso Hachimangū|Q3109957|qid=Q3109957}} as another candidate for Takamu Shrine.From the {{ill|Edo period|ar|فترة إيدو|ast|Periodu Edo|az|Edo dövrü|bcl|Panahon nin Edo|be|Перыяд Эда|bg|Едо (период)|bn|এদো যুগ|bo|ཨེ་དོའི་དུས་སྐབས།|br|Marevezh Edo|ca|Període Edo|ckb|سەردەمی ئێدۆ|cs|Období Edo|cv|Эдо тапхăрĕ|da|Edo-perioden|de|Edo-Zeit|eo|Epoko de Edo|es|Período Edo|et|Edo ajastu|eu|Edo aroa|fa|دوره ادو|fi|Edo-kausi|fr|Époque d'Edo|gl|Período Edo|he|תקופת אדו|hi|एदो अवधी|hr|Edo (razdoblje)|hu|Edo-kor|id|Zaman Edo|is|Jedótímabilið|it|Periodo Edo|ja|江戸時代|jv|Jaman Édo|ko|에도 시대|lt|Edo laikotarpis|lv|Edo periods|mk|Едо (период)|mn|Эдогийн эрин|ms|Zaman Edo|nl|Edoperiode|nn|Edotida|oc|Periòde Edo|pl|Edo (okres)|pt|Período Edo|ro|Perioada Edo|ru|Период Эдо|simple|Edo period|sk|Obdobie Edo|sl|Obdobje Edo|sq|Periudha Edo|sr|Едо период|su|Période Edo|sv|Edoperioden|th|ยุคเอโดะ|tl|Panahong Edo|tok|tenpo pi kulupu lawa Eto|tr|Edo Dönemi|uk|Період Едо|ur|ایڈو دور|uz|Edo davri|vi|Thời kỳ Edo|war|Panahon Edo|wuu|江戶時代|zh|江户时代|zh_min_nan|Edo sî-tāi|zh_yue|江戶時代|qid=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} onward, ``Takamu'' was nicknamed {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=hoko}}, a symbol of {{ill|Weapon|Q728|qid=Q728}}, and a theory spread that it was the site of the armory of the {{ill|Mononobe clan|Q1755836|qid=Q1755836}}, according to the <ref> historical site information board in the temple grounds (established by the Nagoya City Board of Education). </ref>{{Sfn|History of Chikusa Ward|1981|p=33}}{{Sfn|History of Chikusa Ward|1987|p=428}}, "{{ill|Owari Kokunai Jinmyōchō|Q11041830|qid=Q11041830}}" established at the end of the Heian period. Since it is written as ``Takamuku Tenjin,'' it was originally read as ``Takamuku'' and may be related to {{ill|Takamukai clan|Q109357793|qid=Q109357793}} or {{ill|Takamuku Shrine|Q11668968|qid=Q11668968}}.

=== Others ===``Visiting three shrines of love'' includes {{ill|Yamada Tenmangū|Q3571407|qid=Q3571407}} ({{ill|Kita-ku, Nagoya|Q1207964|qid=Q1207964|lt=Kita Ward}}Yamada Town), {{ill|Shiroyama Hachimangū|Q3482375|qid=Q3482375}} (Chikusa Ward{{ill|Shiroyama Town|Q24876539|qid=Q24876539|lt=Shiroyama Town}}), it is a {{ill|Pilgrimage|Q1644573|qid=Q1644573}} spot for fulfilling love. |publisher=Nagoya Tourism and Convention Bureau |accessdate=2016-03-18}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|Japanese book|date= |url=http://www.shiroyama.or.jp/sansyameguri.htm |title=Three shrines of love |publisher=Shiroyama Hachimangu Shrine |accessdate=2016-03-18}}</ref>. Originally planned in {{ill|2002|Q1987|qid=Q1987}} ({{ill|Heisei era|Q234510|qid=Q234510}}14) as a club activity of {{ill|Ohka Gakuen High School|Q11538202|qid=Q11538202|lt=Ohka Gakuen High School}} It became widely known when {{ill|Central Japan Railway Company|Q513679|qid=Q513679|lt=JR Central}} featured it as a walking event in {{ill|2008|Q2004|qid=Q2004}} (Heisei 20). In addition, there were originally three shrines: {{ill|Nagoya Seimei Shrine|Q17229502|qid=Q17229502}} (Chikusa Ward {{ill|Seimeiyama|Q17221162|qid=Q17221162}}), Takamu Shrine, and Shiroyama Hachiman Shrine. Guri Visiting 3 Shrines to Fulfill Love Planned by Ohka Gakuen High School Students, Event on 26th'', {{ill|Mainichi Shimbun|Q1136866|qid=Q1136866}}Morning edition, May 1, 2007, local edition/Aichi, page 20</ref><ref>Natsumi Ikai "Aichi's Archaeological Music, Takamu Shrine, Chikusa Ward, Nagoya City, The Legend of Healing Illness in the Water in the Water", {{ill|Chunichi Shimbun|Q904678|qid=Q904678}}Morning edition, citizen edition, December 13, 2008, p. 19</ref><ref>Ken Shiobara, Sansha Get love by visiting? High school students plan, quietly booming in Chikusa, Nagoya”, {{ill|The Asahi Shimbun|Q720503|qid=Q720503}} Evening edition, February 3, 2012 (Nagoya headquarters edition), p. 7</ref><ref>{{Cite web|Japanese book|url=http://opi-rina.chunichi.co.jp/tankentai/20100128_jinja.html |title=Pray for love fulfillment at three shrines related to love (Opi Exploration Team) |publisher= Chunichi Shimbun Web |date=2010-01-28 |accessdate=2016-03-18}}</ref>.There is an old well within the temple grounds, which is still used for {{ill|Chōzuya|Q1069667|qid=Q1069667}}. It is also the origin of its other name, ``Furui Hachiman,'' as well as the former name of the town where it is enshrined, ``Motofuruimachi,'' and the name of a nearby place, ``Koi no Saka.''

The plaque on the shrine's shrine is based on {{ill|written|qid=written|lt=written}} by {{ill|Nobusuke Kishi|Q315572|qid=Q315572}}.
